explanation: Electric vehicles forced technicians to learn entirely new skills and made the industry rethink its training, so the old mechanical-only approach was overturned, or "upended." "Standardized" would mean the approach became more uniform, which is the opposite of a complete rethinking. "Preceded" and "misrepresented" don't describe how a new technology disrupts an existing practice.

A full ectotherm's body stays at the water temperature, but the basking shark stays 1.0 to 1.5°C warmer, so the finding conflicts with, or is "incongruous with," that classification. The next sentence about a "reevaluation" confirms the mismatch. "Indicative of" is tempting but says the reverse: that the data support the old label.

Because the industry uses very little water overall, its growth is unlikely to make global water scarcity worse, or "exacerbate" it; in South Korea, though, competition for already scarce water means it could. "Assuage" (ease) is the opposite of what the South Korea example shows. "Rescind" and "extricate" don't fit with water scarcity as an object.

The older view treated Appalachian ballads as stand-ins for colonial-era British music, ignoring local changes; newer scholarship fixes that mistake by acknowledging Appalachian innovations and Black spirituals. Something that fixes an error is a "corrective." A "recapitulation" would merely restate the old view, and a "corollary" would follow from it rather than revise it.

The text contrasts Wada, who used European methods, with Hashimoto, who used pigments on silk and preserved centuries-old techniques, so Hashimoto stuck to, or "adhered to," Japanese approaches. "Refrained from" says the opposite. "Reprimanded" and "awarded" make no sense with "approaches" as the object.

Ramchand notes "guiltily" that all the other assistants were already at work at ten in the morning, which suggests he feels bad about arriving later than they did. Nothing indicates he is overwhelmed (A) or excited (B); the other assistants' smiles are described as "fixed," not enthusiastic. He watches the jalabi being made, but the text doesn't present him as fascinated (D).

The lower floors must hold up the weight of the floors above, so a better material for them would compress less over time. If the concrete-based building ended up several inches shorter, the concrete floors were squeezed more, which supports the claim that steel is more suitable. Choices B and D show the steel building performing worse, which would weaken the hypothesis.

The text reports that Trueba et al. didn't find the density/water-stress link seen in earlier studies and then explains why: their rainforest plants came from similar habitats, so trait values varied only a little. That matches explaining an apparent absence of a known association in a homogeneous sample. D overstates this by saying the relationship "cannot be observed," and B wrongly says the earlier finding was invalidated.

The researcher needs a lake whose ice duration increased. Lake Baikal went from about 95 days of ice in 1980–81 to about 110 days in 2005–06, an increase. Choice A fails because Kalmarinjärvi dropped from about 200 to about 150 days, and B and C only state single-year values without showing any change over time.

If REM sleep were homeostatically regulated, every seal should show extra REM sleep after weeks of near-zero REM sleep in the water. The graph shows Seal B dropping to about 90% of baseline on day 2 and Seal C at about 95% on day 1, so the rebound was not consistent. The graph has no data on REM sleep in the water (D) or on differences in baseline levels (B).

Text 1 calls Asimov's characters flat, but Text 2 argues that his thin characterization is deliberate: by focusing less on individuals, he shows that individuals don't matter across centuries of history. So Text 2's author would call the flatness a conscious choice that serves an important idea. Text 2 never compares Asimov to historians (A) and never says Foundation's characters are richer (C).

fix.passage:
Text 1
Isaac Asimov, author of Nemesis and The Stars, Like Dust, is highly regarded despite his mediocre writing style. His prose is workmanlike; <u>his characters are flat and discuss ideas rather than emotions</u>. That this work is enjoyable despite this is a testament to his prodigious imagination—even if people read his books only for the ideas, they will have plenty to consider.

Text 2
Asimov is critiqued for his style, but it is wrong to fault a writer for failing to do what he never intended to do. For example, although most of his novel Foundation consists of people discussing science and politics and we find out little about his characters’ lives, Asimov wanted to convey the vast sweep of human history over centuries, and one of his points is that at such a timescale, individuals don’t matter. Thus his lack of characterization is central to Asimov’s thematic aims.

explanation: The last sentence says the researchers found that gratitude letter and best possible self had the most consistent benefits. Satisfaction processes was reviewed but not singled out (C, D). "Fostering a positive mindset" is a benefit, not a writing method (A).

The hypothesis is that the hot oval was thrown out of the auroral region toward the equator. Time-lapse data showing the oval drifting away from the auroral area over several hours would show exactly that movement. Choice A is about when the oval formed, not where it came from, and B and D describe overall temperature patterns rather than the oval's motion.

Mellaart estimated the population from how densely the mud-brick buildings were packed, assuming they were all homes. The new findings show that many buildings were lived in only briefly or used for storage, so the number of buildings doesn't reliably show how many people lived there at once. The text doesn't discuss mud bricks as a clue to building use (B), and A misstates what the findings challenge.

The critic says the lullaby simply drew the infants' attention. If greater attention usually makes pupils grow larger, then the infants' shrinking pupils point away from increased attention and toward relaxation, which weakens the critic. Choice C tests familiarity, not attention versus relaxation, and D brings in blinking, which the study didn't measure.

The opening phrase, "A recipient of the Nobel Prize...," describes a person, so the noun right after the comma must be that person: chemist Ahmed Zewail. Choice A puts Zewail first and gives him an active verb. Choices B, C, and D begin with "the result," "the limits," or "the introduction," which makes it sound as if those things won the prizes (a dangling modifier).

The subject is the long infinitive phrase "To experience both... and...," which has no main verb yet. An infinitive-phrase subject is singular, so it takes "is": "To experience... is to realize the rich history." Choice C uses the plural "are" because the phrase mentions two things, but it is still one action, and A and B leave the sentence without a main verb.

The first sentence places the series in "the first half of the twentieth century," and the second gives the precise years, 1913 to 1933. A transition that introduces more precise detail is "To be exact." There's no contrast here, so "By contrast" and "Nevertheless" don't fit.

Wee Pals was syndicated in 1965, and the strips mentioned next came out in 1989 and 2008, so the second sentence describes later events. "Later" marks that time order. "Previously" reverses the order, and "For example" doesn't fit because the later strips aren't examples of Turner's first.

The first sentence gives a general aim (analyzing diet composition), and the second narrows it to the ratio of three plant types. "Specifically" introduces this more precise version of the same aim. "Instead" wrongly suggests a different aim replaced the first one.

The second sentence backs up the claim that Ternate was an important port by explaining how its location made it a center of the clove and nutmeg trade. "Indeed" introduces this kind of supporting emphasis. "As a result" is tempting, but Ternate's location was a cause of its importance, not a result of it.

The first sentence says many mushrooms contain phenolic compounds such as protocatechuic acid and biochanin; the second names specific mushrooms where each was found. That is an illustration of the general claim, so "For example" fits. "For this reason" wrongly suggests a cause-and-effect link.

After repeated failed attempts, scientists "later" found the real cause: the soil lacked the fungi the tree needs. "Eventually" marks that the discovery came after a long stretch of failures. There is no comparison or contrast here, so "Similarly" and "In contrast" don't fit.

After 60,000 years ago only gypsum formed, and gypsum points to dry, evaporative conditions without the vegetation that calcite needs. So even though groundwater rose, the climate was arid, which means the higher water levels probably did not come from more local rain. Bennu material kept in very dry nitrogen had plenty of sodium evaporites, but samples lost them after months in ordinary humid air. Choice C ignores this explanation, and D contradicts the finding that the dry storage did preserve the evaporites.

"African Americans" is a plain plural noun (no ownership), and "elections" is also a plain plural, the thing they won. So neither word needs an apostrophe. The other choices add possessive apostrophes where nothing is owned.

The sentence lists three things the museum features, and the first item already contains commas (carvings, textiles, and paintings). A comma (A) would blur the items together, and a period (B) would cut the list in half.

"Having 13,199 feet of prominence" describes the mountain, so the subject right after the comma must be Mount Rainier. Choice C does that. In A, B, and D the subject is "geographers," "the list," or "the ranking," none of which has prominence, so the modifier dangles.

The sentence describes completed past actions and is joined to "gave it the name... in a 2017 YouTube interview," which is in the simple past. "Popularized" keeps the verbs parallel. "Had popularized" would place the action before another past event, which the sentence doesn't set up, and "has popularized" clashes with the past-tense "gave."

"Paleogeneticist Emrah Kırdök" is a title plus a name working as one unit, so no commas go around the name. It is also the first half of the compound subject "Kırdök and his colleagues," and a single comma should never separate the subject from the rest of the sentence. So no punctuation is needed. Choice C adds a comma between the two parts of the subject.
note: Source (model) answer was C; C wrongly puts a comma inside the compound subject "Kırdök and his colleagues".

Most of the observed females spread their eggs across dozens of other ducks' nests, but female 7F64B visited only a few sites and then incubated her own eggs, a different strategy. "Alternatively" introduces this other option. "For example" and "in particular" would wrongly make her a case of the behavior just described, and "similarly" would wrongly signal likeness.

The graph of 2^x curves upward (concave up), so a line crossing it twice lies above the curve only between the two intersection points. Since g is increasing and j < k, the points are ordered a < b, so g(x) > f(x) exactly when a < x < b. Choice C describes where the curve is above the line.
